title: ADR: P2-D SaaS 多租户 3-策略架构
content:
本页镜像自 kun 仓库 docs/architecture/adr-p2d-multitenancy.md（v2026.10.25）。Kun 文档与代码不一致处以代码为准（ADR-001 D1.8）；Qian 对 Kun 的选用与约束见与 Qian 的关系。改动请提到 kun 仓库。

Status: Part 1 Accepted (2026-04-23) · Part 2 Accepted (2026-04-23) · Part 3 Accepted (2026-04-23)
Phase: 2 （白皮书 §12.2 乘风破浪）
Scope: Kun.Core.MultiTenancy + Kun.EntityFrameworkCore.MultiTenancy（未来）
Supersedes: 无（增量于 P0-3 schema-per-service、P1-4 TenantRlsTransactionInterceptor、既有 ITenantContext）

Context

白皮书 §12.2 承诺 v1.5 提供 SaaS 多租户完整方案（共享库 / 独立 Schema / 独立库 三种隔离策略）。当前 (2026-04-23 develop) 已有的多租户基础件是：

组件	位置	用途
ITenantContext	src/Kun.Core/MultiTenancy/ITenantContext.cs	抽象，返回 TenantId / IsMultiTenant
NullTenantContext	同上	非多租户宿主或后台任务
JwtTenantContext（非本 ADR 范围）	Kun.Security	HTTP/gRPC 请求时从 S2S JWT claim 抽
IMultiTenant 全局过滤器	KunDbContext.OnModelCreating	对 IMultiTenant 实体自动追加 e.TenantId == ctx.TenantId 过滤
TenantRlsTransactionInterceptor	src/Kun.EntityFrameworkCore/Interceptors/	每笔事务开启时 SELECT set_config('app.current_tenant_id', @t, true)，用 Postgres RLS 做 defence-in-depth
AddKunTenantRls() 扩展	src/Kun.EntityFrameworkCore/DependencyInjection/KunEntityFrameworkCoreServiceCollectionExtensions.cs	消费者显式开启 RLS 拦截器

现实情况：上面的组合 = Shared 策略（所有租户同库同 schema，用 TenantId 列 + RLS 双层防御）。它已落地并通过 Sprint 1 集成测试。

Phase 2 要补的是两条真正的新策略：

Schema-per-tenant：同库不同 schema，每个 tenant 有独立 schema；

Database-per-tenant：每 tenant 独立连接字符串与独立数据库实例。

两者都需要新的运行时基础件：DbContext 实例化工厂、模型缓存键、迁移调度、连接解析。

Decision

D1. Shared 策略 = 现有 AddKunTenantRls + IMultiTenant 全局过滤器（不新加包装 API）

不引入 AddKunMultiTenancy(Strategy=Shared) 之类的包装扩展来"统一入口"。现有 AddKunTenantRls() 已经是惯用、已公开 API；再套一层 strategy-flag 会让消费者在两个完全等价的入口之间选择。这是 YAGNI 原则 —— 多策略 API 只有在 2+ 策略同时落地时才有实际价值。

Part 2（SchemaPerTenant）落地时再评估是否需要新增 AddKunMultiTenancy(Strategy=…) 作为 "multi-entry dispatcher"；届时 Shared 路径可以委托到现有 AddKunTenantRls 而不破坏任何现有 consumer。

D2. TenantIsolationStrategy 枚举 NOW 落地（forward-looking 类型）

即使当前只有 Shared 可用，Kun.Core.MultiTenancy.TenantIsolationStrategy { Shared, SchemaPerTenant, DatabasePerTenant } 枚举在 Part 1 就落地。理由：

消费者选型文档需要这个稳定的词汇表（docs/guides/saas-multitenancy.md 的决策树）；

未来 ITenantProvisioner / ITenantDbContextFactory 签名会引用它；

枚举是零运行成本的前瞻 API，不会增加维护负担。

Part 2 / Part 3 未交付前，SchemaPerTenant / DatabasePerTenant 值有"定义但未实现"的语义。文档显式声明。

D3. DbContext 实例化模型（按策略分叉）

策略	DbContext 作用域	模型缓存键
Shared	Scoped（现状，EF Core 默认）	默认 IModelCacheKeyFactory（按 Type 键）
SchemaPerTenant（Part 2）	Scoped + 需要 ITenantDbContextFactory<TContext> 在 scope 起始时用当前 ITenantContext.TenantId 构建正确的 MigrationsHistoryTable.Schema 与 DefaultSchema	必须提供自定义 IModelCacheKeyFactory，把 TenantId 并入缓存键，否则第二个租户复用第一个租户的模型 → schema 错位
DatabasePerTenant（Part 3）	Scoped + IDbConnectionResolver 在 OnConfiguring 时用 ITenantContext.TenantId 解析连接字符串	默认 IModelCacheKeyFactory 即可（模型结构相同，只换连接）

D4. 迁移调度模型（按策略分叉）

策略	迁移触发时机	谁来发起
Shared	App 启动时 context.Database.MigrateAsync()（或部署流水线手工）	宿主
SchemaPerTenant	租户开户时通过 ITenantProvisioner.ProvisionAsync(new TenantInfo(tenantId)) 触发；实现内部切到该租户 schema 做迁移	ITenantProvisioner 实现
DatabasePerTenant	租户开户时通过 ITenantProvisioner.ProvisionAsync 触发；实现先创建数据库/连接、再运行迁移	ITenantProvisioner 实现

App-start 批量迁移对 Schema/DatabasePerTenant 不适用（启动时可能尚未注册所有租户，或租户是运行时动态创建）。

D5. 租户生命周期接口 ITenantProvisioner

Part 1 定义契约：

public interface ITenantProvisioner
{
    Task ProvisionAsync(TenantInfo tenant, CancellationToken ct = default);
    Task DeprovisionAsync(string tenantId, CancellationToken ct = default);
}

幂等性约定：ProvisionAsync 重复调用必须无副作用（用 CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS / CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS 语义）。

Null 实现默认：NullTenantProvisioner 两个方法都返回 Task.CompletedTask，让 Shared 策略的消费者不用写空实现。

Part 2 / Part 3 才提供非空实现：SchemaPerTenantProvisioner / DatabasePerTenantProvisioner。

D6. DI 生命周期规则

组件	生命周期	原因
ITenantContext	Scoped	按请求/消息绑定（现状）
ITenantProvisioner	Singleton	无状态，仅依赖配置与日志
ITenantDbContextFactory<TContext> (Part 2)	Scoped	依赖 scoped ITenantContext
IDbConnectionResolver (Part 3)	Singleton（或 Scoped，取决于实现是否需要 scoped 依赖）	默认 Singleton

Alternatives Considered

A1. "为 Shared 加一个 AddKunMultiTenancy(Strategy=Shared) 包装入口，与 Part 2/3 对齐"

拒绝：YAGNI。现有 AddKunTenantRls 已经是稳定 API，加包装只会让消费者选择困扰。Part 2 / Part 3 要上线时 AddKunMultiTenancy 才有 2+ 策略可选，那时再评估。

A2. "用特性/反射自动发现 ITenantProvisioner 实现"

拒绝：违反本仓库 CLAUDE.md 的 AOT-first 原则；显式 DI 注册与强约定足够清晰。

A3. "SchemaPerTenant 通过动态 SET search_path 替代 DefaultSchema"

拒绝（推迟到 Part 2 再讨论）：search_path 切换的事务语义与 RLS + PgBouncer 交互复杂，需要 Part 2 集成测试验证；此时先在 ADR 记录为 open question。

A4. "Database-per-tenant 在单一 DbContext 实例内通过 Database.SetConnectionString 运行时切换"

拒绝（推迟到 Part 3 再讨论）：EF Core 对运行时切连接的模型缓存语义不稳定；更可能的路径是 ITenantDbContextFactory 每次从池里按 tenant 取一个已绑定连接的实例。

Consequences

Positive

Shared 策略消费者零破坏：现有 AddKunTenantRls 签名与行为不变。

Part 1 完全无运行时耦合：4 个新类型都是纯契约，Kun.Core 的零第三方依赖约束保持。

Part 2 / Part 3 的实现者有稳定的目标契约（TenantIsolationStrategy 枚举 + ITenantProvisioner 接口）。

Negative

TenantIsolationStrategy.SchemaPerTenant / .DatabasePerTenant 在 Part 2 / Part 3 前属于"定义但未实现"的值。消费者若提前用会在未来策略 dispatcher 里拿到 NotSupportedException。Part 2 落地时这个语义会被解除。

ITenantProvisioner 的生命周期钩子（开户/注销）与业务域的 tenant onboarding 流程是解耦的；消费者需要自己把这两个调用接到业务流里，框架不做自动编排。

Neutral

现有 NullTenantContext 与新增 NullTenantProvisioner 的"null 对象模式"是仓库的既有风格延伸，不是新约定。

Deferred to Part 2 (SchemaPerTenant)

ITenantDbContextFactory<TContext> 接口定义与实现；

自定义 IModelCacheKeyFactory 把 TenantId 并入缓存键；

SchemaPerTenantProvisioner：CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS "{tenantId}" + 在该 schema 下跑 EF migrations；

KunDbContext 的 OnConfiguring 重载，读取 scoped ITenantContext.TenantId → 调 UseKunSchema；

PgBouncer transaction-pool 兼容性集成测试（schema 切换跨连接的副作用）。

Deferred to Part 3 (DatabasePerTenant)

IDbConnectionResolver 抽象 + 基于 IOptionsMonitor<TenantsConnectionOptions> 的内置实现；

DatabasePerTenantProvisioner：创建数据库 + 跑 migrations + 可选 bootstrap seeding；

跨租户 admin 查询的反模式文档（建议走单独的 AdminDbContext，显式枚举所有连接）；

多区域部署下租户连接发现的运维模式（可选，与 Phase 3 多区域话题挂钩）。

Follow-ups

Part 2 kickoff 单独起 ralplan（SchemaPerTenant 的模型缓存键与迁移时序是需要 consensus 的决策）。

Part 3 kickoff 之前先与运维对齐 secrets 管理（每租户一条连接字符串意味着 secret scale 线性增长）。

当 Part 2 或 Part 3 任一交付时，在 docs/roadmap-p2.md P2-D 章节更新状态，并回补 docs/guides/saas-multitenancy.md 的决策树。

title: ADR-S02: Introduce Kun.Sandbox Module — E2B-compatible sandbox abstraction for Kun consumers
content:
本页镜像自 kun 仓库 docs/architecture/ADR-S02-Kun.Sandbox-module.md（v2026.10.25）。Kun 文档与代码不一致处以代码为准（ADR-001 D1.8）；Qian 对 Kun 的选用与约束见与 Qian 的关系。改动请提到 kun 仓库。

Status: Accepted
Date: 2026-04-23
Author: claude-kun (Kun framework specialist)
Related specs:

NeuroAgent_Sandbox_Spec_v1.1.md §2 / §4 / §14 (E2B-compatible surface)

ADR-S01-E2B-compatible-API.md (Supervisor REST API adopts E2B v2 shape)

1. Context

NeuroAgent is building a self-hosted Sandbox Supervisor that exposes an
E2B-compatible REST API (see ADR-S01). The Python harness
(neuroagent-python) will drive that Supervisor through an E2B-style
SDK. But sandbox usage is not a Python-only concern: the C# business
services in neuroagent-csharp have first-class "run this code / run
this command / produce these files" scenarios that today are pushed up
to the Python harness even when the business logic lives in .NET:

Platform: data preprocessing — ingest + transform uploaded CSV/XLSX
into normalised parquet/JSON before handing to analysts.

Edge: document render — run weasyprint / pandoc to convert
reports generated by C# business logic.

Platform: lightweight one-off scripts — tenant-supplied validation
rules or transform functions that must execute in isolation.

Notification: chart render — headless Chromium to turn a
dashboard snapshot into a PNG attached to an email.

These flows currently have three bad options:

Round-trip through the Python harness — the C# service calls the
Python agent service just to borrow a sandbox. Extra hop, extra auth
surface, harness tooling is agent-centric not service-centric.

Each .NET service reinvents a Supervisor HTTP client — drift,
duplicated auth / retry / tracing logic, each service has to learn
the E2B v2 schema from scratch.

Run code directly in the service process — unacceptable: no
isolation, no egress control, no tenant-scoped audit.

The framework layer is the correct place to unify this. Kun already
owns other horizontal infrastructures consumers rely on
(Kun.EventBus, Kun.Storage, Kun.Identity, …); sandbox execution
is the same category: an abstraction with pluggable backends and a
stable surface.

At the same time, ADR-S01 established E2B v2 as the canonical REST
shape for the Supervisor. The .NET abstraction should mirror that
shape exactly so that (a) the code reads the same as the Python SDK,
(b) future migration to E2B Cloud is equally cheap for .NET consumers,
and (c) nothing in Kun.Sandbox becomes a competing abstraction
relative to the Supervisor spec.

2. Problem

Provide a .NET-idiomatic sandbox abstraction that:

Lets any C# service in neuroagent-csharp (or a future Kun consumer)
create sandboxes, run processes, read/write files, and kill
sandboxes — without knowing whether the backend is a local stub, the
self-hosted Supervisor, or E2B Cloud.

Aligns the interface contract 1-to-1 with the E2B v2 API shape
(endpoints, fields, camelCase JSON), so consumers who already learned
the Python SDK can read .NET call sites unchanged.

Preserves Kun's AOT / zero-reflection posture — callable from
Kun.Gateway, Kun.AspNetCore, or any AOT-strict service.

Does not ship a runtime. The runtime lives in
neuroagent-python/sandbox_supervisor (Python, per Spec v1.1 §14).
Kun.Sandbox is abstraction + client.

3. Decision Drivers

D1 — consumer parity: C# services must have the same sandbox
ergonomics the Python harness already enjoys. Today they don't.

D2 — no drift from the Supervisor spec: every divergence between
the .NET contract and the Supervisor REST contract is a future bug.

D3 — E2B Cloud path preserved: if Mode D (ADR-S01 §14.4) is ever
adopted, .NET consumers should migrate by flipping a registration
line, not by rewriting call sites.

D4 — AOT strict: .NET services in this repo publish AOT.
Sandbox client code must not introduce runtime reflection.

D5 — testability: unit tests for business code that calls a
sandbox must not require Docker; an in-memory provider must exist.

4. Options Considered

Option 1 — No Kun module; each C# service writes its own Supervisor client

Rejected. Directly violates D1 / D2. Guarantees drift. Every
consumer re-learns the E2B schema.

Option 2 — Kun hosts the runtime (port the Python Supervisor into .NET)

Rejected. The Supervisor runtime is deliberately owned by
neuroagent-python because it manages Docker / gVisor / Envoy /
Browser CDP proxying — all concerns where the Python ecosystem is
stronger and the team's existing ops playbook is already invested.
Re-implementing in .NET gives no consumer value, doubles the operational
surface, and violates Spec v1.1 §14 "Supervisor is Python".

Option 3 — Kun ships a thin abstraction + client, backends are pluggable (✅ selected)

Selected. Kun.Sandbox contains:

Abstractions — ISandboxProvider, ISandboxHandle, IProcesses,
IFiles, and request/response records whose fields mirror the E2B v2
REST shape one-to-one (camelCase at the JSON boundary, .NET-idiomatic
PascalCase in code via JsonPropertyName on records).

Implementations (pluggable):
InMemorySandboxProvider — fake for unit tests; no Docker, no network.

SupervisorSandboxProvider — HTTP client against
/v2/sandboxes/* on the NeuroAgent Supervisor (Phase 1 production path).

E2BCloudSandboxProvider — skeleton that throws NotImplementedException;
to be filled in when Phase 2+ Mode D is actually scoped.


DI — services.AddKunSandbox(opts => opts.UseSupervisor(url, cert) | opts.UseE2BCloud(key, team) | opts.UseInMemory()).

5. Decision

Adopt Option 3. The framework layer gains a new module:

src/Kun.Sandbox/
  Kun.Sandbox.csproj             (IsAotCandidate=true)
  AGENTS.md
  Abstractions/
    ISandboxProvider.cs
    ISandboxHandle.cs
    IProcesses.cs
    IFiles.cs
    SandboxCreateOptions.cs
    ProcessRunOptions.cs
    ProcessResult.cs
    FileEntry.cs
  Implementations/
    InMemorySandboxProvider.cs
    SupervisorSandboxProvider.cs
    E2BCloudSandboxProvider.cs
  Extensions/
    ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs
  Internal/
    SandboxJsonContext.cs        (source-generated JSON for AOT)

The interface contract is "the E2B v2 API in C# records":

ISandboxProvider.CreateAsync(SandboxCreateOptions, CT) maps to
POST /v2/sandboxes.

ISandboxHandle.Processes.RunAsync(cmd, ProcessRunOptions, CT) maps
to POST /v2/sandboxes/{id}/processes.

ISandboxHandle.Files.ReadAsync/WriteAsync/ListAsync/DeleteAsync
map to GET/POST/GET .../list/DELETE /v2/sandboxes/{id}/files (with
?path= query parameters per Spec v1.1 §4.5).

ISandboxHandle.KillAsync() maps to
DELETE /v2/sandboxes/{id}.

Record fields carry [JsonPropertyName] attributes that emit
camelCase at the JSON boundary (matching E2B) while keeping
idiomatic PascalCase inside the .NET code. NeuroAgent extensions
(secret scope, browser, egress, max commands) live under a
NeuroagentExtension property on SandboxCreateOptions serialised as
the neuroagent sub-object — exactly mirroring the spec.

6. Consequences

Positive

C# business services can directly consume sandboxes through a
typed, AOT-friendly API without learning HTTP / E2B schemas inline.

The abstraction is backend-agnostic: swapping
UseSupervisor → UseE2BCloud is a one-line change when Mode D is
scoped.

Unit tests can use InMemorySandboxProvider with no Docker
dependency.

The interface contract is the E2B v2 shape, so .NET call sites and
Python SDK call sites read the same — lower cognitive load for
engineers crossing stacks.

Negative / Trade-offs

Kun.Sandbox must track E2B v2 API evolution. Mitigation: monitor
E2B changelog (same rule as ADR-S01). Breaking changes cascade
through Kun.Sandbox to all consumers; that is intended.

Kun.Sandbox does not own a runtime. Any expectation that a
local UseInMemory() provides real isolation is wrong — it is a test
fake. AGENTS.md and XML docs are explicit about this.

The Supervisor client path requires S2S JWT + mTLS to the Supervisor.
Callers must wire Kun.Security (or an equivalent S2S token source)
into the HttpClient via a DelegatingHandler. Docs show the
canonical wiring.

Risks

Risk	Mitigation
Consumer drifts the record shape away from E2B schema	CI contract test: SandboxCreateOptions / ProcessResult JSON output diffed against a golden fixture derived from E2B v2 docs; diff > 0 fails the build.
InMemorySandboxProvider leaks into production wiring	AddKunSandbox + UseInMemory name signals "test only"; AGENTS.md calls it out; follow-up can add a KUN_SANDBOX_ALLOW_INMEMORY_IN_PROD=false guard if abuse appears.
Supervisor upgrades a field shape mid-flight	Records use [JsonPropertyName] + JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull so additive changes are backward-compatible; breaking changes require an explicit version bump.
E2B Cloud provider is tempting to "finish early"	The stub throws NotImplementedException with a clear message. Filling it requires a dedicated task after Mode D is scoped — not a drive-by.

7. Alternatives not taken

Owning the runtime in .NET (Option 2): rejected; Supervisor is Python
by design.

A single provider that branches internally on BackendKind: rejected;
three explicit implementations are clearer and each can carry its own
dependencies / tests.

Exposing raw HttpClient with helper methods: rejected; would force
every consumer to re-derive the URL shape and undermine the
abstraction's reason for existing.

8. Validation

Spec alignment: SandboxCreateOptions JSON payload (camelCase,
cpuCount/memoryMB/timeoutMs/envs/metadata/neuroagent.*)
matches the request body in Spec v1.1 §4.3 byte-for-byte.

AOT: CI AOT-publish matrix adds Kun.Sandbox and runs
dotnet publish -p:PublishAot=true /warnaserror with zero warnings.

Tests: tests/Kun.Sandbox.Tests/ includes ≥ 15 tests (in-memory
lifecycle, Supervisor request-shape via WireMock.Net, E2B-Cloud stub
surface, DI options round-trip, camelCase serialisation, parallel
sandbox isolation).

9. References

ADR-S01-E2B-compatible-API.md (parent, Supervisor REST shape)

NeuroAgent_Sandbox_Spec_v1.1.md §§1.3, 2, 4, 12, 14, 17

ADR-009-Kun.Configuration-module.md (sibling example of an
Abstraction-layer module with pluggable backends)

E2B Cloud API docs — tracked external
contract this module mirrors

toc.text: Option 1 — No Kun module; each C# service writes its own Supervisor client
Option 2 — Kun hosts the *runtime* (port the Python Supervisor into .NET)
Option 3 — Kun ships a thin abstraction + client, backends are pluggable (✅ selected)

title: When to use ICurrentUser vs IAuthenticatedUser
content:
本页镜像自 kun 仓库 docs/architecture/when-to-use-currentuser.md（v2026.10.25）。Kun 文档与代码不一致处以代码为准（ADR-001 D1.8）；Qian 对 Kun 的选用与约束见与 Qian 的关系。改动请提到 kun 仓库。

Status: guidance (not an ADR — implements the direction set in
ADR-008 and
ADR-010)
Last touched: 2026-10-25 (S1-KUN-017：端口登记与次序)

Kun Framework exposes two user-context interfaces. They are not
competing abstractions — they are layered, with
IAuthenticatedUser inheriting ICurrentUser. The DI registration
in Kun.Identity.AspNetCore binds both to the same
request-scoped instance, so the choice of injected interface is
purely about the fields a given caller needs.

This doc exists to answer the next sprint's question before anyone
invents a third adapter.

Current state

Kun.Core.Security.ICurrentUser           ← minimal, S2S JWT-shaped
    │  UserId, Roles, IsAuthenticated, PrincipalKind
    │
    └── Kun.Identity.Abstractions.IAuthenticatedUser
           ← adds browser / cookie concerns
           │  TenantId, Email, Name, Principal

Two runtime bindings ship today:

Binding	Source	Ships as
Kun.Security.JwtCurrentUser	S2S JWT claims	ICurrentUser
Kun.Identity.AspNetCore.KunCurrentUser	Cookie / OIDC code flow	ICurrentUser and IAuthenticatedUser

AnonymousCurrentUser in Kun.Core.Security is the no-auth
sentinel — used by background workers and tests that have no
request context.

Decision table

Caller scenario	Inject	Why
gRPC service handler (S2S JWT)	ICurrentUser	S2S tokens only carry sub + roles; browser fields would always be null.
gRPC interceptor / pipeline behaviour	ICurrentUser	Same — operates at the S2S boundary.
ASP.NET Core API endpoint the browser hits directly	IAuthenticatedUser	Cookie middleware populated TenantId / Email / Name / Principal; skip the cast.
ASP.NET Core background worker (BackgroundService)	ICurrentUser with a null check	No request scope exists; bind AnonymousCurrentUser explicitly.
Outbox / Saga step executor	ICurrentUser, usually AnonymousCurrentUser.	Background context — inherit the S2S identity only if the invoker explicitly pushed it into OTel baggage (see Kun.Observability.Enrichment.KunBaggageKeys).
Unit test	ICurrentUser with a hand-rolled fake (a record MyUser(…) : ICurrentUser) or AnonymousCurrentUser.Instance.	Tests depend only on the narrow interface; no HTTP context is needed.
Component that reads tenant (EF filter, cache key)	ITenantContext, not either of these.	Tenant identity propagation has its own abstraction — don't couple persistence-layer code to an auth interface.

How to extend correctly

Happens rarely. When you need a new field:

Is it present on S2S JWT claims? → add to ICurrentUser and
to every implementation. Update
docs/architecture/ADR-008-Kun.Identity-module.md with the
rationale.

Is it browser / cookie only? → add to IAuthenticatedUser.
Update docs/architecture/ADR-010-Kun.Identity-cookie-session.md.

Is it a concern of a different subsystem? (tracing, tenancy,
feature flags) → add it to the subsystem's own abstraction
(ITenantContext, ITracedCurrentUser, …) and have the
current-user binding expose or forward it there if needed.
Example precedent: ITracedCurrentUser carries TraceId without
polluting ICurrentUser.

Anti-patterns (do not do these)

❌ ICurrentUserEx / IEnhancedCurrentUser / ICurrentUserV2 —
every one of these reinvents IAuthenticatedUser. If
IAuthenticatedUser is missing a field, add the field to
IAuthenticatedUser after reading ADR-010, don't fork.

❌ A per-service ICurrentUser subinterface in
neuroagent-csharp (or any downstream consumer) — consumer
services get no value from owning the abstraction.

❌ ClaimsPrincipal injection as a first-class service —
always go through IAuthenticatedUser.Principal. Direct
ClaimsPrincipal injection hides which host provided it.

❌ Mutable ICurrentUser implementations — instances are
scoped to a single request; mutating one breaks baggage
assumptions for the async context.

❌ Making ICurrentUser depend on
Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.HttpContext — Kun.Core is BCL-only
and the interface stays there so non-HTTP hosts (gRPC-only
workers, integration tests) can target it without ASP.NET Core
in their closure.

If you think you need something new

Read this doc end-to-end. Yes, including the anti-patterns.

Read ADR-008 and ADR-010.

Post the proposed field + its source (JWT claim / cookie /
header / derived) in the PR description and call out which
interface it belongs to per the decision rules above.

If none of the rules fit, write an ADR that supersedes / extends
ADR-010 with the new concern — before adding code.

If the addition is still ambiguous after all that, leave the code
as-is and raise it at the next framework review. The cost of one
extra sprint of "injecting IAuthenticatedUser and casting to
something" is far lower than the cost of shipping a third
sibling abstraction that every downstream service then has to
track.

授权主体类型

PrincipalKind 是 principal_kind 的只读身份投影。内置 JWT / Cookie 适配器与 HTTP/gRPC 权限入口使用同一个主身份读取规则，Mediator 从 ICurrentUser 取值。不能从调用请求的 JSON、头或角色名推断它。旧自定义适配器默认 user；如果适配器代表服务或 Agent，必须显式实现此属性，不能让机器身份继续使用用户默认值。

端口登记与次序

ICurrentUser 与 ITenantContext 只由身份 / 多租户适配器登记：AddKunSecurity()（JwtCurrentUser、AsyncLocalTenantContext）、AddKunIdentityAspNetCore()（KunCurrentUser）、AddKunMultiTenancy()，或宿主自己的适配器。数据与审计组件不占这两个端口：AddKunDataConventions<TContext>() 与 AddKunAuditing<TContext>() 的拦截器在上下文创建时按需解析，没有登记时按匿名（AnonymousCurrentUser）、无租户（NullTenantContext）记录。所以适配器在数据组件之前或之后登记都生效，不存在「先登记数据组件就把身份适配器挤掉」的次序约束。

AddKunSecurity()、AddKunIdentityAspNetCore() 以 TryAdd 登记：同一宿主装了多个真实适配器时先登记者生效，要换实现就显式 Replace；AddKunMultiTenancy() 以 Add 登记租户端口，覆盖之前的登记。

宿主自己的服务构造注入 ICurrentUser、而宿主又没有身份适配器时（后台作业、迁移任务），显式登记 AnonymousCurrentUser.Instance；框架不再顺带替它登记。

KunDbContext 的构造需要 ITenantContext：单租户宿主显式登记 NullTenantContext.Instance。

title: Why Kun Splits Writes from Reads
content:
本页镜像自 kun 仓库 docs/architecture/why-cqrs.md（v2026.10.25）。Kun 文档与代码不一致处以代码为准（ADR-001 D1.8）；Qian 对 Kun 的选用与约束见与 Qian 的关系。改动请提到 kun 仓库。

Kun enforces a hard boundary between the write side and the read side of every bounded context.
This is not a stylistic preference — it is enforced by module dependencies and verified by CI.
Understanding the reasoning helps you work within the model rather than against it.

The write side: consistency first

Command handlers run against EF Core through KunDbContext and the repository and specification
abstractions in Kun.Infrastructure. The write side loads an aggregate, calls domain methods,
and delegates to IUnitOfWork.SaveChangesAsync. That single call does several things atomically:

Applies EF Core change tracking to produce the correct SQL.

Collects domain events from every modified IAggregateRoot via ChangeTracker.

Dispatches domain events to in-process handlers via IDomainEventDispatcher.

Converts any resulting integration events into OutboxMessage rows.

Commits the aggregate changes and the Outbox rows in one database transaction.

This sequence exists because consistency is the write side's job. A command either fully
succeeds — business state updated, domain events dispatched, integration events enqueued — or
it fully fails with no observable side-effects. The Specification pattern keeps query logic out of
handler code while still letting the repository translate rich criteria into SQL without leaking
EF Core types up into the domain layer.

The cost is performance. Loading aggregates, tracking changes, and running the full pipeline
takes more work per request than a raw SQL insert. For the write side this is the correct
trade-off: correctness matters more than throughput.

The read side: performance first

Query handlers use Kun.Dapper — specifically IReadDbConnectionFactory, which opens a
dedicated read connection (potentially to a read replica). Queries are raw SQL annotated with
[DapperAot] so Dapper's source generator produces the mapping code at compile time. No EF
Core context is involved; there is no change tracker, no aggregate loading, no domain logic.

The result is flat DTOs returned directly to the caller. Because there is no object graph to
navigate and no invariants to enforce, the read side can denormalize freely: a single query can
join five tables and return a DTO shaped exactly for the API response, avoiding the N+1 problems
that appear when EF Core navigation properties are misused.

AOT compatibility is a direct benefit. Kun.Dapper is an AOT candidate module. The
[DapperAot] annotation tells the Dapper source generator to emit the reader code at build time,
eliminating the reflection that Dapper's classic Query<T> relies on. The read side is therefore
both faster at runtime and publishable as a native AOT binary.

How the Command/Query divide maps to Kun.Mediator

KunMediator dispatches every IRequest<TResponse> to its registered handler through a
FrozenDictionary<Type, RequestHandlerBase> — O(1) lookup with zero runtime reflection. Handlers
are registered explicitly at startup via KunMediatorBuilder. The mediator does not scan
assemblies; there is no runtime discovery.

Pipeline behaviors wrap each dispatch. The standard write-side stack is:

ValidationPipelineBehavior   ← rejects invalid commands before touching the database
UnitOfWorkPipelineBehavior   ← calls SaveChangesAsync after the handler returns
LoggingBehavior              ← structured log at entry and exit
TracingBehavior              ← opens an OpenTelemetry span per dispatch

Query handlers carry only LoggingBehavior and TracingBehavior by default — there is nothing
to validate or commit. Adding UnitOfWorkPipelineBehavior to a query handler is a configuration
mistake that the type system cannot prevent, but CI code review does. The distinction is
explicit: every registration in Program.cs names the request type, the response type, and the
handler type. There is no magic.

Trade-offs to be aware of

Two models to maintain. Every write-side aggregate and its corresponding read-side DTO are
separate representations. When you add a field to an aggregate you must also update any queries
and DTOs that need to surface it. The consistency guarantee you get from the write side does not
automatically flow to the read side.

Denormalization can drift. Read-side DTOs are shaped for API consumers, not normalized from
aggregate state. If a consumer's requirements change and the DTO is updated but the underlying
data is not re-projected, the read side and the write side can express different views of the
same entity.

No EF Core in query handlers. Using EF Core in a query handler breaks the UoW pipeline
behavior's transaction boundary assumptions and bypasses the AOT guarantee of the read-side path.
This is not enforced by the compiler, but Kun.Dapper depends on Kun.Infrastructure and not
on Kun.EntityFrameworkCore, so adding an EF Core dependency to a query handler requires a
deliberate csproj change that reviewers will catch.

The split is explicit and by design. It makes each side independently optimizable and keeps the
invariants of each clearly scoped.

title: Why Kun Uses the Outbox Pattern
content:
本页镜像自 kun 仓库 docs/architecture/why-outbox.md（v2026.10.25）。Kun 文档与代码不一致处以代码为准（ADR-001 D1.8）；Qian 对 Kun 的选用与约束见与 Qian 的关系。改动请提到 kun 仓库。

When a service saves a business entity and publishes an integration event, those are two separate
I/O operations. The Outbox pattern exists to make them behave as one. This document explains the
problem, Kun's solution, and the trade-offs you accept.

The dual-write problem

Consider the naive approach to event publishing:

await dbContext.SaveChangesAsync();          // (1) aggregate persisted
await broker.PublishAsync(integrationEvent); // (2) event published to RabbitMQ

These two operations are not atomic. Any failure between (1) and (2) leaves the system
inconsistent: the database reflects the new state but consumers never learn about it. Retrying
(1) is unsafe — it may double-write. Putting (2) before (1) has the mirror problem: the event
fires but the database write fails.

Worse, the broker itself is a network dependency. A transient RabbitMQ outage at step (2) means
lost events with no recovery path — unless you build one yourself. That recovery logic is exactly
what the Outbox pattern provides.

How Kun atomizes the publish

Kun's write-side pipeline centers on EfUnitOfWork.SaveChangesAsync. The sequence inside that
method is:

Domain events are collected from ChangeTracker.Entries<IAggregateRoot>() and dispatched
in-process via IDomainEventDispatcher.

In-process domain event handlers call IIntegrationEventBus.Publish, which stages the
integration event in the IntegrationEventBuffer — an in-memory accumulator scoped to the
current request.

Each staged event is converted to an OutboxMessage row. The stable event type identifier
(e.g. product.published.v1) is resolved from IEventTypeRegistry — never from
Type.AssemblyQualifiedName, which would break across assembly renames and refactors.

The payload is serialized via KunJsonContext.Default.GetTypeInfo(type), which uses a
source-generated JsonSerializerContext. No runtime reflection; safe for AOT.

Activity.Current?.Id and Activity.Current?.TraceStateString are captured as TraceParent
and TraceState on the message so the trace can be resumed on the other side of the broker.

DbContext.SaveChangesAsync commits the aggregate changes and the OutboxMessage rows in a
single database transaction.

Because step 6 is one transaction, either both the business state and the Outbox row are
committed, or neither is. The dual-write problem is eliminated.

How the background publisher drains the Outbox

OutboxPublisherBackgroundService is a BackgroundService that runs in every process that has
the Outbox registered. On each scan cycle it:

Queries OutboxMessage rows with Status = Pending, ordered by OccurredAt.

For each message, restores the W3C trace context from TraceParent/TraceState to link the
publish span to the original request trace.

Calls IIntegrationEventPublisher.PublishAsync — in production this is the RabbitMQ
publisher from Kun.EventBus.RabbitMQ; in the Order sample it is a no-op that logs to
stdout.

On success: calls OutboxMessage.MarkPublished and saves.

On failure: increments AttemptCount, records LastError, and retries with exponential
back-off. After the configured maximum attempts the message transitions to Failed and
requires manual intervention.

The scan uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (or a Redis distributed lock) so multiple
instances of the same service do not race on the same batch.

Consumer idempotency via IProcessedMessageStore

Because the publisher uses at-least-once delivery — the broker acknowledgement and the database
MarkPublished update are still two operations — a consumer may receive the same message more
than once. Every consumer handler is wrapped in IdempotentConsumerDecorator<T>, which checks
IProcessedMessageStore before invoking the handler.

The default implementation uses Redis SETNX with a TTL (default 30 minutes) keyed on
idemp:{consumerName}:{messageId}. If the key already exists the message is acknowledged and
discarded. Consumer handlers must still be written to be safe when called more than once, but the
decorator handles the common case without requiring every handler to implement its own
deduplication.

Trade-offs to be aware of

Latency is measured in seconds, not milliseconds. The background publisher runs on a polling
interval. A consumer will see an event seconds after the originating transaction commits, not
sub-millisecond. If your design requires synchronous cross-service consistency, the Outbox is not
the right tool — gRPC calls with Result-based error handling are.

The Outbox store requires a reliable database. The pattern works because the database is the
source of truth for pending messages. If the database is unavailable, no messages are published —
but this is safer than losing messages silently. Recovery is automatic once the database is
reachable again.

Failed messages need a recovery workflow. Messages that exhaust retries end up in the
Failed state. There is no automatic dead-letter re-queue for failed Outbox messages; you need
an operational process to inspect, correct, and republish them.

The Outbox pattern adds operational surface area in exchange for a guarantee that the dual-write
problem cannot silently corrupt your system state. That trade is almost always worth making in a
distributed system where correctness matters.

See also

ADR-015 Outbox pattern design — full design walk-through: type
surface, atomicity boundary, publisher pump, consumer idempotency, rejected alternatives.

kun/CLAUDE.md §Outbox — normative rules (atomicity, stable event IDs, idempotent consumers,
W3C trace propagation). The rules constrain; this primer explains the problem; the ADR explains
the design.

title: Why Kun Uses Saga Orchestration
content:
本页镜像自 kun 仓库 docs/architecture/why-saga.md（v2026.10.25）。Kun 文档与代码不一致处以代码为准（ADR-001 D1.8）；Qian 对 Kun 的选用与约束见与 Qian 的关系。改动请提到 kun 仓库。

Distributed transactions cannot use database-level locking across service boundaries. Sagas
replace the two-phase commit with a sequence of local transactions, each of which can be
compensated if a later step fails. Kun implements this as Orchestration — a central coordinator
rather than services reacting to each other's events. This document explains the choice and what
it costs.

The problem: multi-step distributed work

Consider an order placement flow: reserve inventory in Catalog, charge the customer via Payment,
hand off to Shipping, then notify the customer. Each step touches a different service and a
different database. A failure at step 3 means steps 1 and 2 have already committed and must be
explicitly reversed. Without a coordinator, determining what to reverse and in what order requires
every service to understand the global workflow — which it cannot do without coupling.

Orchestration vs. Choreography

Choreography places no central coordinator. Each service publishes events and reacts to
events from others. The workflow is implicit in the event topology. This works well for simple,
stable flows but becomes difficult to debug when something goes wrong: tracing a failure requires
reconstructing the event sequence across multiple services and topics, and adding a step means
modifying the event contracts of multiple services simultaneously.

Orchestration places a central coordinator — in Kun, SagaOrchestrator — that knows the
complete step list and drives execution. Each service executes a step when instructed and reports
success or failure. The coordinator decides what comes next.

Kun chose Orchestration for three concrete reasons:

Failure recovery is explicit. When step N fails, the orchestrator knows it must
compensate steps N-1 down to 0 in reverse order. This logic lives in one place — the
ISaga<TContext> definition — rather than being inferred from event reactions scattered across
services.

State is inspectable. Every SagaInstance is a row in the saga_instances table with a
State column (Running, Compensating, Completed, Compensated, Failed) and a
CurrentStepIndex. A plain SQL query tells you exactly where every in-flight saga is. In
choreography the equivalent requires correlating event logs from multiple topics.

Compensation order is deterministic. Kun's SagaStepExecutor compensates from the failed
step index backwards, one entry per saga_step_queue row. The order is guaranteed by the
queue, not by the timing of event delivery.

The three recovery paths

Happy path. SagaStepExecutor polls saga_step_queue, calls ExecuteAsync on each entry,
and on success enqueues the next step. When the last step succeeds the instance transitions to
Completed.

Failure compensation. When ExecuteAsync throws SagaStepFailedException, the executor
transitions the instance to Compensating and enqueues CompensateAsync calls from the failed
step index back to step 0. Compensation runs through the same polling loop. The instance ends as
Compensated.

Timeout compensation. SagaTimeoutDetector scans every 5 seconds for instances where
TimeoutAt < UtcNow AND State = Running. On a match it calls SagaInstance.StartCompensating
and enqueues the same reverse entries the failure path would produce. In the Order sample,
ShipOrderStep has a 10-second timeout override; the saga default is 30 seconds.

Idempotency is mandatory

Every CompensateAsync must be safe to call more than once. The saga_step_queue table tracks
ProcessedAt to prevent the executor from processing the same entry twice, but a crash between
processing and marking can cause a re-run. A compensation that checks aggregate state before
acting — "cancel the order only if its status is Paid" — is idempotent. One that unconditionally
issues a refund is not. The same requirement applies to ExecuteAsync.

The Order sample (samples/Kun.Sample.Order) is the concrete reference: PlaceOrderCommandHandler
calls ISagaOrchestrator.StartAsync<OrderCreationSaga, OrderCreationSagaContext>(), which
persists the SagaInstance and the first queue entry in the same EF Core transaction as the
Order row. The saga cannot be partially started.

Trade-offs to be aware of

Coupling to the coordinator. Every step must be registered with the orchestrator. The step
list in the ISaga<TContext> definition couples the coordinator to each participant's expected
behavior. You cannot add a participant without modifying that list.

State must be modeled explicitly. The saga context carries all shared state as a serializable
payload. Anything a step needs from a previous step must be stored there — more work than implicit
event-driven state, but also visible and auditable.

No distributed lock across step execution. The executor relies on SKIP LOCKED to avoid
races between instances. If your database does not support SKIP LOCKED (PostgreSQL does;
older MySQL does not), step idempotency is the only safety net.

Orchestration adds a coordinator as a point of coupling. In exchange it gives you deterministic
failure recovery, a single inspectable state table, and no ambiguity about compensation order.

title: Getting Started with Kun Framework
content:
本页镜像自 kun 仓库 docs/getting-started.md（v2026.10.25）。Kun 文档与代码不一致处以代码为准（ADR-001 D1.8）；Qian 对 Kun 的选用与约束见与 Qian 的关系。改动请提到 kun 仓库。

This tutorial takes about 10 minutes. By the end you will have the full sample stack running
locally, have triggered all three saga paths (happy, failure compensation, timeout compensation),
and have a mental model of how the pieces fit together.

Prerequisites

Requirement	Version	Notes
.NET SDK	10.0.100 or later	Pinned in global.json
Docker Desktop	Any recent stable	Runs PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, Redis containers
Aspire workload	Installed via dotnet workload	See step below
Visual Studio Build Tools (Windows only)	Optional	Required only for AOT native publish

Verify your SDK version:

dotnet --version
# must print 10.0.100 or higher

Verify Docker is running:

docker info
# must succeed — no "Cannot connect" errors

Install the Aspire workload

The AppHost project uses .NET Aspire to orchestrate all containers and services. Install the
workload once per machine:

dotnet workload install aspire

If the workload was already installed and you want to update it:

dotnet workload update

Clone and build

git clone https://github.com/idadawn/kun.git
cd kun
dotnet restore
dotnet build -c Release

A successful build produces zero errors. Warnings about AOT trimming in Kun.EntityFrameworkCore
are expected and acceptable — that module is deliberately marked trim-safe rather than AOT.

Run the test suite to confirm everything is green:

dotnet test -c Release --no-build

Run the samples

The AppHost project starts every service and all required infrastructure with a single command:

dotnet run --project samples/Kun.Sample.AppHost

Aspire prints a dashboard URL to the console, typically:

Login to the dashboard at: http://localhost:15888

Open that URL in a browser. You will see the Aspire Dashboard with:

Panel	What it shows
Resources	Live health of catalog, order, gateway, postgres, rabbitmq, redis
Logs	Structured log streams per service, filterable by level
Traces	Distributed OpenTelemetry traces across all service boundaries
Metrics	Request rates, latency histograms, CPU and memory

Wait until all resources in the Resources panel show a green status indicator before sending
requests. PostgreSQL runs schema creation (EnsureCreated) at startup, which takes a few seconds.

Find the service ports

The Order service port is dynamic — Aspire assigns it at startup. In the Dashboard:

Click Resources.

Find the order row.

Copy the URL from the Endpoints column, for example http://localhost:54321.

Use that base URL in the curl commands below. The examples use $ORDER as a placeholder:

# Set this to the URL shown in the Aspire Dashboard for the "order" resource
ORDER=http://localhost:54321

Walk through a happy-path order

Send a POST request to create an order that succeeds all four saga steps:

curl -s -X POST "$ORDER/demo/happy-path" | jq .

Example response:

{
  "orderId": "3fa85f64-5717-4562-b3fc-2c963f66afa6",
  "path": "happy-path"
}

Copy the orderId value. Query the saga state:

curl -s "$ORDER/demo/sagas/3fa85f64-5717-4562-b3fc-2c963f66afa6" | jq .

The response includes the current SagaInstance state. Immediately after the POST the saga is
Running as the background SagaStepExecutor works through the steps. Poll a few seconds later
and the state transitions to Completed:

{
  "sagaId": "3fa85f64-5717-4562-b3fc-2c963f66afa6",
  "state": "Completed",
  "currentStepIndex": 3,
  "failureReason": null
}

What happened:

PlaceOrderCommand handler created an Order row and called ISagaOrchestrator.StartAsync.

The orchestrator inserted a saga_instances row (state Running) and the first
saga_step_queue entry — all inside the same EF Core transaction as the Order row.

The background SagaStepExecutor picked up the queue entry and ran each step in order:
Step 0 ReserveInventoryStep — logs "would gRPC Catalog", sets order status Reserved

Step 1 ProcessPaymentStep — sets order status Paid

Step 2 ShipOrderStep — sets order status Shipped

Step 3 NotifyCustomerStep — sets order status Completed, enqueues order.completed.v1
via the Outbox


SagaInstance.State was set to Completed.

Open Traces in the Aspire Dashboard and filter by order. You will see a single root trace
with child spans for each saga step, the EF Core queries, and the Outbox publish.

Trigger the compensation path

This demonstrates what happens when a saga step fails: the orchestrator runs compensation steps
in reverse order.

curl -s -X POST "$ORDER/demo/trigger-payment-failure" | jq .

Response:

{
  "orderId": "...",
  "path": "payment-failure",
  "note": "Saga will compensate ReserveInventory."
}

Query the saga state a moment later:

curl -s "$ORDER/demo/sagas/<orderId>" | jq .

Expected final state:

{
  "sagaId": "...",
  "state": "Compensated",
  "currentStepIndex": 1,
  "failureReason": "ProcessPaymentStep failed: simulated payment failure"
}

What happened:

ProcessPaymentStep detected SimulateFailure = "payment" in the saga context and threw
SagaStepFailedException.

The executor set SagaInstance.State to Compensating and enqueued CompensateAsync calls
for steps 1 and 0 in reverse order.

ProcessPaymentStep.CompensateAsync — cancels the order if status is Paid

ReserveInventoryStep.CompensateAsync — cancels the order (idempotent)

Final state: Compensated.

In the Aspire Dashboard Traces view you will see saga.step.execute spans for steps 0 and 1,
followed by saga.step.compensate spans for steps 1 and 0 in reverse.

Trigger the timeout path

This demonstrates the SagaTimeoutDetector background service, which scans for stuck steps
every 5 seconds and kicks off compensation automatically.

curl -s -X POST "$ORDER/demo/trigger-timeout" | jq .

Response:

{
  "orderId": "...",
  "path": "timeout",
  "note": "ShipOrderStep sleeps 60s — SagaTimeoutDetector compensates."
}

ShipOrderStep is configured with a 10-second per-step timeout override. When the step sleeps
for 60 seconds the SagaTimeoutDetector wakes up, finds the instance past its TimeoutAt
deadline, and triggers compensation from the current step index backwards.

After roughly 10–15 seconds:

curl -s "$ORDER/demo/sagas/<orderId>" | jq .

Expected:

{
  "sagaId": "...",
  "state": "Compensated",
  "currentStepIndex": 2,
  "failureReason": "Step 2 timed out at ..."
}

What you just saw

All three paths exercised the same underlying building blocks:

Outbox transactional publishing — every saga start and every integration event enqueue
happened inside a single EF Core SaveChangesAsync call. If the database transaction rolled back,
no message was produced. The OutboxPublisherBackgroundService drains Pending rows to the
broker asynchronously, so publish latency is measured in seconds but consistency is guaranteed.

Saga orchestration — the SagaOrchestrator is a central coordinator. It persists all state
in saga_instances and saga_step_queue tables, making the current state inspectable with a
plain SQL query at any time. There is no implicit choreography happening via event reactions.

W3C Trace Context propagation — every OutboxMessage row stores the traceparent and
tracestate headers captured at enqueue time. The background publisher resumes the trace when it
publishes, so a single TraceId threads through HTTP ingress → CQRS handler → Outbox → broker
→ consumer → downstream saga steps. This is visible in the Aspire Dashboard Traces panel.

Next steps

Simpler CQRS story — samples/Kun.Sample.Catalog/ demonstrates DDD aggregates, write/read
split with EF Core and Dapper, and Outbox event publishing without any saga involvement. Its
README walks through the file structure.

Architecture essays — understand the design trade-offs:
Why CQRS?

Why Outbox?

Why Saga Orchestration?


Module map — docs/architecture/module-map.md shows the
full dependency graph and which modules are AOT candidates.

CLAUDE.md — the binding architectural rules that every code contribution must satisfy,
including the four-layer dependency constraint and AOT restrictions.

title: Gateway 限流策略指南
content:
本页镜像自 kun 仓库 docs/guides/gateway-rate-limit.md（v2026.10.25）。Kun 文档与代码不一致处以代码为准（ADR-001 D1.8）；Qian 对 Kun 的选用与约束见与 Qian 的关系。改动请提到 kun 仓库。

Kun.Gateway.RateLimiting 把 ASP.NET Core 内置的 RateLimiter 包装成策略 × 分区的两维组合：
三种分区解析（partition resolver）× 三种限流策略（limiter policy）= 九种可选配置，配合 Redis 后端做跨 Pod 计数共享。
参考：docs/architecture/why-cqrs.md · 白皮书 §12.2

分区解析 (IRateLimitPartitionResolver)

决定"同一个限流桶由谁共享"。从 HttpContext 里取一个字符串 key。

实现	分区依据	适用
IpRateLimitPartitionResolver	HttpContext.Connection.RemoteIpAddress	匿名 API、防 abuse
TenantRateLimitPartitionResolver	已验证外部 JWT 的 tenant_id claim	多租户共享库场景（默认）
UserPrincipalRateLimitPartitionResolver	已验证外部 JWT 的 sub claim	Free-tier API，per-account 限额

注册：任意一种用 services.AddSingleton<IRateLimitPartitionResolver, XxxResolver>()。Kun 的 AddKunXxxRateLimiter() 系列扩展会用 TryAddSingleton<...,TenantRateLimitPartitionResolver>() 做默认，你预先注册就覆盖它。

限流策略 (IRateLimiterPolicy)

决定"桶里怎么发放许可"。

策略	行为	特点	默认值
FixedWindow（AddKunRateLimiter）	每 N 秒重置计数	最简单、内存最低，边界突刺	100 permits / 1 min
SlidingWindow（AddKunSlidingWindowRateLimiter）	分段滑动	平滑，无突刺；内存与 SegmentsPerWindow 线性	100 / 1 min / 6 segments
TokenBucket（AddKunTokenBucketRateLimiter）	令牌累积 + 匀速补充	吸收突发流量；适合 webhook fanout、批量导入	100 tokens burst，20 / 10s 补充

三者均调用 AddRateLimiter() 注册一个具名策略："kun-default"、"kun-sliding-window"、"kun-token-bucket"。端点开启时写：

app.MapGet("/orders", handler).RequireRateLimiting(KunRateLimiterExtensions.SlidingWindowPolicyName);

网关默认边界

AddKunGateway() 已注册 kun-default，并为未显式设置 RateLimiterPolicy 的 YARP 路由绑定它。业务路由同时默认要求认证；只有配置 AuthorizationPolicy: "Anonymous" 的路由可匿名访问。普通 ASP.NET 端点仍需调用上面的 RequireRateLimiting。三种内置策略超限均返回 429；限流器提供重试时间时，响应附整数秒 Retry-After。具名自定义策略也沿用默认拒绝回调，除非宿主显式覆盖。

IP 分区仅读取 Connection.RemoteIpAddress。宿主须在认证和限流之前调用 UseForwardedHeaders()；独立网关已接好。KunGateway.TrustedProxyAddresses（IP 列表）和 TrustedProxyNetworks（CIDR 列表）只填写实际反向代理出口，ForwardLimit 默认 1。两张名单均为空时关闭转发头处理，非信任来源伪造 X-Forwarded-For 不会切换限流桶。不要单独清空框架的 KnownProxies/KnownIPNetworks：框架会将其理解为信任全部。

典型组合

1. 多租户 SaaS，边界精度要求一般

builder.Services.AddKunRateLimiter();   // Tenant partition + FixedWindow

2. 按用户限流，平滑曲线

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IRateLimitPartitionResolver, UserPrincipalRateLimitPartitionResolver>();
builder.Services.AddKunSlidingWindowRateLimiter(o => { o.PermitLimit = 60; o.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1); });

3. 防 DDoS 按 IP，允许突发

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IRateLimitPartitionResolver, IpRateLimitPartitionResolver>();
builder.Services.AddKunTokenBucketRateLimiter(o =>
{
    o.TokenLimit = 500;
    o.TokensPerPeriod = 50;
    o.ReplenishmentPeriod = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1);   // 50 req/s 稳态
});

Redis 后端：跨 Pod 分布式计数

内置的 FixedWindow / SlidingWindow / TokenBucket 策略都是进程内（每个 Gateway pod 各自独立计数）。在多 pod 部署时 100 permits 会变成 100 × podCount 的实际吞吐。

Kun.Gateway.RateLimiting.IRedisRateLimitStore 提供基础 primitive：

services.AddSingleton<IConnectionMultiplexer>(ConnectionMultiplexer.Connect("redis:6379"));
services.AddKunRedisRateLimitStore(o => o.KeyPrefix = "kun:prod:rl");

调用：

var result = await store.HitAsync("tenant-a", TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1));
// result.Count 现在有多少个命中、result.ResetsIn 距离重置还有多久
if (result.Count > 100) { /* reject */ }

实现要点：

原子 INCR，首次命中额外 EXPIRE 设 TTL，后续命中不触发 EXPIRE（保持滑动边界）

计数器自动到期自清理，无需后台 GC 任务

多 Pod 共享计数，PgBouncer / Redis Cluster 环境里行为一致

限制：当前 RedisFixedWindowRateLimitStore 是低层 primitive，不是 PartitionedRateLimiter<HttpContext> 实现。即你不能直接用 RequireRateLimiting("redis-policy") 让框架路由到它；需要手写一个 middleware 调 HitAsync 并在命中超限时返回 429。框架内置 PartitionedRateLimiter 适配留待未来（tracked as Part 3b）。

落地 checklist

选一个 IRateLimitPartitionResolver（或默认 Tenant）

选一个或多个限流策略（AddKunXxxRateLimiter）

在需要的端点调 .RequireRateLimiting(KunRateLimiterExtensions.XxxPolicyName)

多 Pod 部署：额外注册 AddKunRedisRateLimitStore + 写 middleware 替代/补强

压测：推荐 Testcontainers.Redis + 100 并发 request，校验精度 < 2% drift

title: Schema-per-service with KunDbContext
content:
本页镜像自 kun 仓库 docs/schema-per-service.md（v2026.10.25）。Kun 文档与代码不一致处以代码为准（ADR-001 D1.8）；Qian 对 Kun 的选用与约束见与 Qian 的关系。改动请提到 kun 仓库。

Scope: how to run multiple Kun-based services against a single PostgreSQL
instance by giving each service its own schema (catalog, order, …), with
business tables, the Outbox, Saga tables, and the EF migrations-history table
all co-located under that schema.
Applies to: any KunDbContext-derived DbContext using Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL.
Last updated: 2026-04-22.

Why schema-per-service

Running many services against one physical Postgres instance is operationally
cheap (one cluster to patch, one backup path, one connection pool). But putting
everything in public makes name collisions inevitable — two services both want
an outbox_messages, an __ef_migrations_history, and so on.

Kun's answer: each service overrides KunDbContext.DefaultSchema with its own
name ("catalog", "order", etc.), and UseKunSchema(schema) on the options
builder wires the migrations-history table into the same schema. A
SchemaConsistencyInterceptor then fails fast at the first SaveChangesAsync
if the two ever disagree, so misconfigurations surface in dev instead of
silently leaking rows across schemas in production.

End-to-end recipe

1. Override DefaultSchema on your DbContext

using Kun.Core.MultiTenancy;
using Kun.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

public sealed class CatalogDbContext : KunDbContext
{
    public DbSet<Product> Products => Set<Product>();

    public CatalogDbContext(
        DbContextOptions<CatalogDbContext> options,
        ITenantContext tenantContext)
        : base(options, tenantContext)
    {
    }

    /// <inheritdoc/>
    protected override string? DefaultSchema => "catalog";

    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
    {
        base.OnModelCreating(modelBuilder); // applies HasDefaultSchema(DefaultSchema)
        modelBuilder.ApplyConfiguration(new ProductConfiguration());
    }
}

KunDbContext.OnModelCreating calls modelBuilder.HasDefaultSchema(DefaultSchema)
before applying the Outbox and tenant-filter configurations, so every
unqualified .ToTable("x") lands under catalog.

2. Chain UseKunSchema("catalog") in the design-time factory and DI

The design-time factory drives dotnet ef migrations add:

using Kun.Core.MultiTenancy;
using Kun.EntityFrameworkCore.Extensions; // UseKunSchema lives here
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design;

internal sealed class CatalogDesignTimeFactory
    : IDesignTimeDbContextFactory<CatalogDbContext>
{
    public CatalogDbContext CreateDbContext(string[] args)
    {
        var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<CatalogDbContext>()
            .UseNpgsql("Host=localhost;Database=catalog_design;Username=postgres;Password=postgres")
            .UseKunSchema("catalog")   // wires MigrationsHistoryTableSchema
            .Options;

        return new CatalogDbContext(options, NullTenantContext.Instance);
    }
}

Same pattern in the runtime AddDbContext call:

services.AddDbContext<CatalogDbContext>((_, options) =>
    options
        .UseNpgsql(connectionString)
        .UseKunSchema("catalog"));

Order matters: .UseNpgsql(...) must precede .UseKunSchema(...) so the
relational provider extension already exists by the time UseKunSchema mutates
MigrationsHistoryTableSchema.

3. Regenerate migrations under the new schema

For an existing service already carrying public-schema migrations, regenerate
them once:

# Remove the old public-schema migrations
dotnet ef migrations remove \
  --project samples/Kun.Sample.Catalog \
  --startup-project samples/Kun.Sample.Catalog \
  --force

# Re-add under the new schema — the DesignTimeFactory's UseKunSchema("catalog")
# drives the correct MigrationsHistoryTable schema.
dotnet ef migrations add Initial_SchemaQualified \
  --project samples/Kun.Sample.Catalog \
  --startup-project samples/Kun.Sample.Catalog \
  --output-dir Infrastructure/Migrations

Inspect the generated _Initial_SchemaQualified.cs — every CreateTable /
CreateIndex / DropTable call now carries schema: "catalog", and the
generated ModelSnapshot.cs starts with .HasDefaultSchema("catalog").

Windows / Git Bash note

Both of the commands above must run with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 in Git Bash,
otherwise --project values get path-mangled:

MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 dotnet ef migrations add Initial_SchemaQualified \
  --project samples/Kun.Sample.Catalog \
  --startup-project samples/Kun.Sample.Catalog \
  --output-dir Infrastructure/Migrations

Run the two services' dotnet ef migrations add commands sequentially
(not in parallel) — they compete for the same src/Kun.EntityFrameworkCore
build artefacts.

4. Create the schemas in Postgres

dotnet ef database update will call EnsureSchema("catalog") via the
generated migration, so in most cases you do nothing. For a plain
EnsureCreatedAsync() flow (tests / quick prototyping), EF also issues
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS catalog. You can create the schemas ahead of
time if you want the service accounts to have restricted grants:

CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS catalog;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS "order";  -- note: 'order' is reserved, quote it
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA catalog TO svc_catalog;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA "order" TO svc_order;

5. Verify with dotnet ef migrations list

After migrations regenerate, confirm the history table lives in the right
schema:

dotnet ef migrations list --project samples/Kun.Sample.Catalog
# shows catalog.__ef_migrations_history
dotnet ef migrations list --project samples/Kun.Sample.Order
# shows order.__ef_migrations_history

The safety net: SchemaConsistencyInterceptor

KunDbContext.OnConfiguring unconditionally registers a
SchemaConsistencyInterceptor whose job is exactly one thing: compare
Model.GetDefaultSchema() against the relational provider's
MigrationsHistoryTableSchema at the first SaveChangesAsync, and throw
InvalidOperationException with a remediation hint when they diverge.

This catches the most common error — overriding DefaultSchema on your
DbContext but forgetting to call UseKunSchema(...) on the options builder.
Without the interceptor, business tables would land under catalog while
__ef_migrations_history silently stays in public, a migration-drift
timebomb. With the interceptor, the first save fails loudly:

InvalidOperationException: KunDbContext.DefaultSchema='catalog' does not match
MigrationsHistoryTable schema='(null)'. Call .UseKunSchema("catalog") on
DbContextOptionsBuilder to wire both consistently.

The check is gated by Interlocked.CompareExchange so it runs exactly once
per DbContext instance — zero overhead after the first transaction.

Outbox and Saga co-location

Because the KunDbContext base class applies HasDefaultSchema(DefaultSchema)
before ApplyConfiguration(new OutboxMessageConfiguration()), the Outbox
table inherits the same schema without any extra configuration. Similarly,
Saga tables registered via modelBuilder.ApplyKunSagaConfiguration() land in
the service schema.

This is deliberate — having catalog.outbox_messages in the same schema as
catalog.catalog_products lets a single transaction atomically commit both,
which is the entire point of the Outbox pattern. Putting the outbox in a
shared outbox schema would break that atomicity story (cross-schema writes
still commit atomically, but the operational mental model gets muddier, and
separate grants / backup policies become harder to reason about).

Running multiple services against one PostgreSQL

Once each service has its own schema, they can target the same physical
Postgres instance and the same logical database. Aspire wires this up
trivially — the Kun.Sample.AppHost sample points Catalog and Order at
the same postgres resource:

var postgres = builder.AddPostgres("postgres");
var kun = postgres.AddDatabase("kun");

builder.AddProject<Projects.Kun_Sample_Catalog>("catalog")
    .WithReference(kun);
builder.AddProject<Projects.Kun_Sample_Order>("order")
    .WithReference(kun);

With schema-per-service in place, the two services coexist without name
collisions — each SELECT * FROM catalog.outbox_messages stays well-scoped.

Reference implementation

src/Kun.EntityFrameworkCore/KunDbContext.cs — DefaultSchema virtual
property + auto-registration of the interceptor.

src/Kun.EntityFrameworkCore/Extensions/KunDbContextOptionsBuilderExtensions.cs —
the UseKunSchema extension.

src/Kun.EntityFrameworkCore/Interceptors/SchemaConsistencyInterceptor.cs —
the fail-fast guard.

samples/Kun.Sample.Catalog/Infrastructure/CatalogDbContext.cs + migrations —
concrete example with a catalog schema.

samples/Kun.Sample.Order/Infrastructure/OrderDbContext.cs + migrations —
concrete example with an order schema (plus Saga tables).

tests/Kun.IntegrationTests/Persistence/SchemaPerServiceTests.cs —
Testcontainers-backed test that boots two KunDbContext subclasses under
distinct schemas against one Postgres and asserts physical isolation in
information_schema.tables.

title: Tracing Tour: Reading Distributed Traces in the Aspire Dashboard
content:
本页镜像自 kun 仓库 docs/observability/tracing-tour.md（v2026.10.25）。Kun 文档与代码不一致处以代码为准（ADR-001 D1.8）；Qian 对 Kun 的选用与约束见与 Qian 的关系。改动请提到 kun 仓库。

This document walks through the OpenTelemetry traces you will see when running the Kun sample
stack via dotnet run --project samples/Kun.Sample.AppHost. It assumes Docker and the Aspire
workload are installed and the stack is running. For setup instructions see
docs/getting-started.md.

W3C Trace Context and OTLP

Every Kun service propagates traces using the
W3C Trace Context standard. Each in-process span records
a traceparent header that carries the TraceId and SpanId. When a request crosses a process
boundary — HTTP, gRPC, or the Outbox — the receiving side extracts the parent context and creates
a child span under the same TraceId. The result is a single trace tree that spans every hop
from the initial HTTP request to the final consumer acknowledgement.

Spans are exported via OTLP. When running under .NET Aspire the OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
environment variable is set automatically to the Aspire Dashboard's collector endpoint. The
Dashboard collects and renders all spans without any additional configuration in the services
themselves. Framework modules (src/Kun.*) contain no OTel package dependencies — all
AddKunObservability wiring lives in the sample composition root
(samples/Kun.Sample.Shared/OpenTelemetryExtensions.cs) so the framework remains AOT-clean.

What Instruments What

Kun.Mediator

ActivitySource name: Kun.Mediator

TracingBehavior<TRequest, TResponse> wraps every ISender.Send and IPublisher.Publish call
(see src/Kun.Mediator/Behaviors/TracingBehavior.cs). It starts an ActivityKind.Internal span
named Mediator.Send {RequestTypeName} — for example Mediator.Send CreateProductCommand or
Mediator.Send GetProductByIdQuery.

The span is a child of the ambient activity at dispatch time, which is typically the ASP.NET Core
server span for the incoming HTTP request. Because the Mediator span is internal, it appears as a
nested block directly under the HTTP span in the Dashboard timeline.

Tags set on this span:

Tag	Value
(none beyond span name)	The request type name is encoded in the span name

If you want to add custom tags (e.g. command ID, tenant ID), do so from within the handler by
calling Activity.Current?.SetTag(...).

Kun.EventBus.Outbox

ActivitySource name: Kun.EventBus.Outbox

OutboxPublisherBackgroundService starts one ActivityKind.Producer span named outbox.publish
for each OutboxMessage it successfully publishes to the broker (see
src/Kun.EventBus/Background/OutboxPublisherBackgroundService.cs).

The critical detail is that the parent context is restored from the stored row, not from the
current ambient activity. When EfUnitOfWork.SaveChangesAsync writes an OutboxMessage row, the
IntegrationEventOutboxAccumulator captures Activity.Current?.Id and
Activity.Current?.TraceStateString and stores them in the TraceParent and TraceState
columns of the row. The background service reads those columns back hours or seconds later and
calls ActivityContext.TryParse(message.TraceParent, message.TraceState, ...) to reconstruct the
parent context before starting the publish span.

This means the outbox.publish span appears as a child of the original producer span in the
Dashboard, even though it runs in a different process tick, in a different background service
invocation, potentially seconds after the HTTP response was already sent to the client.

Tags set on outbox.publish:

Tag	Value
messaging.system	outbox
messaging.destination	Stable event type ID, e.g. product.published.v1
messaging.message_id	UUID of the OutboxMessage row

Kun.Grpc

ActivitySource name: Kun.Grpc

KunTracingInterceptor (see src/Kun.Grpc/Interceptors/KunTracingInterceptor.cs) runs first in
the interceptor chain registered by AddKunGrpc. It starts an ActivityKind.Server span named
grpc.server for each unary, client-streaming, server-streaming or duplex RPC call. The span
remains active until the awaited handler completes, including all stream operations.

Tags set:

Tag	Value
rpc.system	grpc
rpc.method	Full gRPC method path, e.g. /catalog.CatalogService/GetProduct
rpc.type	unary, client_streaming, server_streaming or duplex_streaming
rpc.grpc.status_code	Final gRPC status code; faults also mark the activity as Error

If a downstream service calls a Kun gRPC service, the caller's HttpClient instruments propagate
the traceparent header via the standard gRPC client instrumentation wired in
AddKunObservability. The server interceptor picks up the parent context automatically from the
incoming metadata — ActivityKind.Server causes the OTel SDK to look for an inbound W3C header.

Kun.Saga

ActivitySource name: Kun.Saga

SagaStepExecutor (see src/Kun.Saga/Orchestration/SagaStepExecutor.cs) starts one
ActivityKind.Internal span per step queue entry it processes. The span name encodes the
direction:

saga.step.execute — forward execution of a step

saga.step.compensate — reverse compensation of a step

Tags set:

Tag	Value
saga.step_index	Zero-based index of the step in the saga definition
saga.saga_id	UUID of the SagaInstance
saga.direction	Execute or Compensate
saga.name	Registered saga class name, e.g. OrderCreationSaga

Note: these spans are started by the SagaStepExecutor background service polling loop. The
background service does not restore a producer trace context from the saga instance row — the
saga spans therefore appear as root spans or under whatever ambient activity the poll loop happens
to inherit. Cross-trace correlation via saga.saga_id is the intended mechanism; see the
saga_id as cross-trace correlation section below.

How to Read a Happy-Path Trace

The happy path is triggered by POST /demo/happy-path against the Order service. This is what
you should see in the Aspire Dashboard Traces panel:

[HTTP POST /demo/happy-path]  ← ASP.NET Core server span (root)
  └─ [Mediator.Send PlaceOrderCommand]  ← TracingBehavior span
       └─ [outbox.publish order.completed.v1]  ← OutboxPublisherBackgroundService span
            (parent context restored from OutboxMessage.TraceParent)

The saga step spans appear separately because the SagaStepExecutor runs in a background
service:

[saga.step.execute]  saga.step_index=0, saga.name=OrderCreationSaga
[saga.step.execute]  saga.step_index=1, saga.name=OrderCreationSaga
[saga.step.execute]  saga.step_index=2, saga.name=OrderCreationSaga
[saga.step.execute]  saga.step_index=3, saga.name=OrderCreationSaga

To correlate these saga step spans with the originating HTTP request, use the saga.saga_id tag
(see the next section). Filter by the saga UUID in the Dashboard search bar to find all spans
associated with a single saga instance.

The timeline for the happy path looks like this in wall-clock order:

POST /demo/happy-path arrives. ASP.NET Core opens a server span.

PlaceOrderCommand is dispatched via ISender.Send. TracingBehavior opens a child span.

The command handler calls ISagaOrchestrator.StartAsync. This writes a SagaInstance row and
the first SagaStepQueueEntry row inside the same EF Core SaveChangesAsync transaction.

The HTTP response is sent. The server span closes.

Seconds later, SagaStepExecutor polls FetchPendingStepsAsync and finds the queue entry.
It opens a saga.step.execute span and runs ReserveInventoryStep.ExecuteAsync. On success,
it enqueues step 1 and marks the entry processed.

Steps 1, 2, and 3 execute in sequence in subsequent poll cycles.

NotifyCustomerStep enqueues an order.completed.v1 OutboxMessage row inside its
SaveChangesAsync call. The TraceParent of the current saga.step.execute span is captured
into the row.

OutboxPublisherBackgroundService polls, finds the pending message, restores the trace
context from TraceParent, and opens an outbox.publish child span. The message is published
to RabbitMQ and the row is marked Published.

In the Dashboard, the outbox.publish span correctly appears as a descendant of the saga step
that produced it, giving you the full causal chain in one view.

How to Read a Compensation Trace

The compensation path is triggered by POST /demo/trigger-payment-failure. The trace structure
reflects the point of failure and the reverse execution:

[HTTP POST /demo/trigger-payment-failure]
  └─ [Mediator.Send PlaceOrderCommand]

Then in background poll cycles:

[saga.step.execute]  step_index=0  (ReserveInventoryStep — succeeds)
[saga.step.execute]  step_index=1  (ProcessPaymentStep — fails, span status=Error)
[saga.step.compensate]  step_index=1  (ProcessPaymentStep.CompensateAsync)
[saga.step.compensate]  step_index=0  (ReserveInventoryStep.CompensateAsync)

When ProcessPaymentStep.ExecuteAsync throws SagaStepFailedException, the executor:

Sets activity?.SetStatus(ActivityStatusCode.Error, ex.Message) on the failing span — visible
as a red span in the Dashboard.

Transitions the SagaInstance to SagaState.Compensating.

Enqueues Compensate entries for steps 1 and 0 in reverse order.

The compensation spans appear with saga.direction=Compensate in their tags. Because they run in
the same background service with the same ActivitySource, they appear in the Dashboard's "all
spans" list alongside the execution spans. Searching by saga.saga_id brings them together.

To distinguish failure from normal completion in the Dashboard:

A saga.step.execute span with ActivityStatus=Error is the failing step.

Following saga.step.compensate spans at lower step_index values are the rollback.

The final SagaInstance.State stored in the database is Compensated.

saga_id as Cross-Trace Correlation

Because saga steps run in a background poll loop that does not inherit the HTTP request's trace
context, each saga step span is technically a separate root trace in OTLP terms. The saga.saga_id
tag set on every step span is the mechanism for correlating them.

In the Aspire Dashboard:

Trigger any demo endpoint and note the sagaId in the response body.

Open Traces and use the attribute search or filter bar to search for
saga.saga_id = <your-uuid>.

All saga.step.execute and saga.step.compensate spans for that saga instance appear,
giving you a complete step-by-step history.

The tag name is saga.saga_id and its value is the SagaInstance.Id UUID. This tag is set in
SagaStepExecutor.ProcessEntryAsync via activity?.SetTag("saga.saga_id", entry.SagaId.ToString()).

Note for contributors: connecting saga step spans back to the originating HTTP trace via a stored
TraceParent on the SagaInstance row — similar to how OutboxMessage does it — would allow
the full saga lifecycle to appear as one unified trace tree. This is not currently implemented
and is tracked as future work.

How to Read Outbox Lag

Outbox lag is the time between when an integration event was enqueued (the producer's
SaveChangesAsync commit) and when it was actually published to the broker (the
outbox.publish span).

To measure lag in the Dashboard:

Find the Mediator.Send span for a command that produces an integration event (e.g.
CreateProductCommand).

Note its end timestamp — this is approximately when SaveChangesAsync committed and the
outbox row was written.

Find the outbox.publish span for the same message (match by messaging.message_id, or by
messaging.destination + approximate time).

The start timestamp of outbox.publish minus the end timestamp of the producer span is
the outbox lag for that message.

Under normal conditions with the default OutboxPublisherOptions.PollInterval of 2 seconds and
BatchSize of 50, lag is typically 0–4 seconds. Under heavy load, lag grows as the batch fills.
Reduce PollInterval or increase BatchSize to tune.

The OutboxPublisherOptions defaults:

Setting	Default	Effect
BatchSize	50	Messages processed per poll cycle
PollInterval	2 seconds	Sleep between cycles when queue is non-empty
MaxAttempts	5	Publish attempts before transitioning row to Failed
RetryBaseDelay	1 second	Exponential backoff base delay

A message in OutboxStatus.Failed will not be retried automatically. Monitor for Failed rows
in the outbox_messages table and alert on them — they represent messages that could not be
delivered after all attempts.

Pitfalls and Common Gaps

Background services that do not start an activity

SagaStepExecutor and OutboxPublisherBackgroundService are BackgroundService implementations.
Their ExecuteAsync loop does not have an ambient Activity unless one is explicitly started.
This means:

Any log message emitted inside the loop but outside a span will have no TraceId attached in
structured logs.

Any child activity started without an explicit parent context appears as a root span in OTLP.

If you add custom background services to your application and want their spans connected to
a broader trace, you must restore the parent context manually — the same pattern used by
OutboxPublisherBackgroundService with ActivityContext.TryParse.

async void timers and fire-and-forget

Avoid async void methods and _ = Task.Run(...) inside handlers or background services.
Exceptions thrown on async void paths crash the process without ending any open spans, leaving
dangling incomplete spans in the Dashboard. Use async Task and await throughout.

Gateway observability

The standalone Kun.Gateway host registers AddKunObservability with service name
kun-gateway, configured through KunObservability. EF instrumentation is disabled because
this host does not access EF. Native AOT hosts must set IncludeEfCore=false; a runtime-feature
guard removes that reflection-based path at link time and rejects attempts to enable it at runtime. ASP.NET request spans cover proxy and JWKS requests, while
HttpClient instrumentation covers downstream calls; there is no separate custom transform span.
The gateway remains in the Native AOT audit. Consumers that reference the gateway package in
their own host choose their own observability registration.

Key span names to recognize at a glance

Span name	Source	Meaning
Mediator.Send {Type}	Kun.Mediator	A command or query was dispatched
outbox.publish	Kun.EventBus.Outbox	An outbox row was published to the broker
grpc.server	Kun.Grpc	A unary or streaming gRPC call was handled
saga.step.execute	Kun.Saga	A saga step ran forward
saga.step.compensate	Kun.Saga	A saga step ran in compensation

title: Kun 框架
content:
本页由 kun 仓库的定位与模块矩阵拼装，来源 README.md（v2026.10.25）。Kun 文档与代码不一致处以代码为准（ADR-001 D1.8）；Qian 对 Kun 的选用与约束见与 Qian 的关系。改动请提到 kun 仓库。

一款为 .NET 10 打造的现代化云原生微服务开发框架

Kun 是 Qian 的底座框架：Qian 平台基于 Kun 框架构建，前端使用 yue 组件库（ADR-021）。本节按仓库 Directory.Packages.props 的 KunVersion 镜像 kun 仓库 v2026.10.25 的文档，与 Qian 实际依赖的 Kun 是同一版本；Kun 的代码与文档改动去 kun 仓库提。

本节内容

与 Qian 的关系：Qian 自写的唯一一页——Kun 模块与平台插件、seam 的对应，canonical API，强制装配与禁用项，补丁包状态

上手：Getting Started with Kun Framework

模块地图：模块地图

指南：Gateway 限流策略指南、Identity 客户端、浏览器会话与迁移、Saga 编排指南（Orchestration）、Outbox + Integration Events 指南、Read-Side Patterns: Writing Query Handlers、SaaS 多租户策略选型指南、Command 校验指南（Kun.Validation）、Tracing Tour: Reading Distributed Traces in the Aspire Dashboard、Schema-per-service with KunDbContext

安全：审计：同事务实体记录与 PostgreSQL 命令哈希链、Multi-Tenancy: Row-Level Security as Defence in Depth、Service-to-Service JWT Authentication

设计说明与 ADR：ADR-001 Do Not Introduce a New Kun.Identity Module、ADR-003 Introduce Kun.Audit and Kun.Audit.EntityFrameworkCore Modules、ADR-004 Introduce Kun.Observability Module、ADR-005 Introduce Kun.Caching Module、ADR-006 Introduce Kun.RateLimit Module、ADR-007 Introduce Kun.MultiTenancy and Kun.MultiTenancy.EntityFrameworkCore Modules、ADR-008 Introduce Kun.Identity Module — Reversing ADR-001、ADR-009 Introduce Kun.Configuration Module、ADR-010 Add Cookie Session + IAuthenticatedUser to Kun.Identity、ADR-011 Result composition extensions (sync + async)、ADR-012 Introduce Kun.Testing module、ADR-013 Baggage-driven activity enricher for Kun.Observability、ADR-014 Result-returning validation pipeline behavior、ADR-015 Outbox pattern design for Kun.EventBus、ADR-016 配置可靠性、权限端口与能力目录、ADR-S02 Introduce Kun.Sandbox Module — E2B-compatible sandbox abstraction for Kun consumers、ADR P2-D SaaS 多租户 3-策略架构、When to use ICurrentUser vs IAuthenticatedUser、Why Kun Splits Writes from Reads、Why Kun Uses the Outbox Pattern、Why Kun Uses Saga Orchestration

白皮书：Kun Framework 架构设计与产品白皮书

变更日志；发布说明：Kun Framework — v0.1.0-phase1

API 参考：DocFX 从 35 个 Kun.* 包生成

模块矩阵

Phase 1 顶层速览（完整矩阵请见 docs/architecture/module-map.md）：

模块	职责	是否 AOT
Kun.Core	领域抽象、CQRS 接口、Result、ITenantContext	✅
Kun.Mediator	FrozenDictionary 无反射调度、Pipeline Behaviors	✅
Kun.Infrastructure	仓储/UoW/规约接口、IProcessedMessageStore	✅
Kun.EntityFrameworkCore	写侧 EF Core 实现、Outbox 落库、租户过滤器	⚠️ trim-safe
Kun.Dapper	读侧 Dapper AOT 封装	⚠️ trim-safe
Kun.EventBus.Abstractions	稳定事件标记与 JSON 注册端口（只依赖 Core）	✅
Kun.EventBus	领域/集成事件抽象、Outbox 发布器	✅
Kun.EventBus.RabbitMQ	RabbitMQ 传输、消费端幂等	✅
Kun.Saga	Saga Orchestration 编排器	⚠️ trim-safe（Phase 2 拆 EF 子模块）
Kun.Security	S2S JWT 签发/校验、租户上下文注入	✅
Kun.Identity	外部 OIDC 客户端、JWT 校验与原子会话	✅
Kun.MultiTenancy	ITenantContext + EF 查询过滤器	✅
Kun.Audit	双通道审计：writer/reader 抽象 + EventBusAuditWriter + SHA-256 哈希链 Mediator Pipeline Behavior	✅
Kun.RateLimit	按租户 / IP 分区限流	✅
Kun.Caching	IKunCache + Memory / Redis 后端	✅
Kun.Storage	7-method IFileStorage + Local / S3 + 活跃-MIME attachment 强制	✅
Kun.Observability	统一 OpenTelemetry 装配：AddKunObservability 一键接入 Kun 全套 ActivitySource + HTTP/EF/Runtime 指令	✅
Kun.Configuration	强类型 Options + fail-fast 校验	✅
Kun.Sandbox	E2B v2 兼容 sandbox + Supervisor / E2B Cloud / InMemory 后端	✅
Kun.Validation	SourceGen 验证器	✅
Kun.AspNetCore	Minimal API 扩展、Pipeline Behaviors	⚠️ trim-safe
Kun.Grpc	gRPC 拦截器、Result→RpcException 映射	✅
Kun.Gateway	YARP 扩展、S2S 签发、限流	✅

title: Changelog
content:
本页镜像自 kun 仓库 CHANGELOG.md（v2026.10.25）。Kun 文档与代码不一致处以代码为准（ADR-001 D1.8）；Qian 对 Kun 的选用与约束见与 Qian 的关系。改动请提到 kun 仓库。

本文档记录 Kun Framework 的所有显著变更。

格式基于 Keep a Changelog。版本号采用 CalVer（vYYYY.M.D[-hotfix.N|-beta.N]，从 main 打 tag，见 CONTRIBUTING.md）；更早的历史条目遵循 Semantic Versioning。

Unreleased

2026.10.25 - 2026-10-25

Fixed — 数据约定与实体审计不再占用当前主体 / 租户端口（S1-KUN-017）

AddKunDataConventions<TContext>() 不再以 TryAdd 把 AnonymousCurrentUser 登记进 ICurrentUser；AuditFieldsSaveChangesInterceptor 改为工厂登记，在上下文创建时按需解析 ICurrentUser，宿主没有身份适配器时仍按匿名写 null。此前宿主先登记数据约定、后调用 AddKunSecurity() 时，后者的 TryAdd 落空，ICurrentUser 恒为匿名：审计字段写 null，比对框架主体的下游（如命令管道）对一切请求判拒。

AddKunAuditing<TContext>() 同样不再登记 NullTenantContext / AnonymousCurrentUser 兜底，TransactionalAuditingSaveChangesInterceptor 按需解析两个端口。此前先登记实体审计、后调用 AddKunSecurity() 时，租户端口落成无租户，审计与 RLS 拿不到请求租户。

公开 API 不变。新增用例覆盖身份适配器在数据约定之前 / 之后登记、以及真实 AddKunSecurity() 晚于数据组件登记时的同事务审计（审计字段与 AuditLog 记令牌主体与租户）；登记次序约定写进 docs/architecture/when-to-use-currentuser.md。

行为变更：框架不再顺带登记这两个端口。没有身份适配器、又在自己的服务里构造注入 ICurrentUser 的宿主（后台作业、迁移任务等），升级后首次解析即报无法解析，须显式登记 AnonymousCurrentUser.Instance；只用 AddKunAuditing<TContext>()、没有任何租户登记的单租户宿主，构造 KunDbContext 时报无法解析 ITenantContext，须显式登记 NullTenantContext.Instance。
